name: Three and a Half Tang Timber Halls
lede: The only Tang-dynasty timber buildings that can still be confirmed in China are three halls in Shanxi. The Amitabha Hall of Tiantai Hermitage in Pingshun was long regarded as Tang, but recent research mostly dates it to the Five Dynasties, so enthusiasts speak of “three and a half.”
note: Four entries correspond to the “three and a half.” Following current research, this catalog places Tiantai Hermitage in the Five Dynasties, but it stays on this list to record the traditional view.
selectionReason: These three Tang halls and the debated Tiantai'an span intimate three-bay buildings and a seven-bay hall. Compare their columns and roofs, and see how inscriptions can change a building's dating.

itemReasons.nanchan: Start with a three-bay hall without interior columns: its simple timber frame leaves an uninterrupted space for worship.
itemReasons.guangren: Turn from Buddhist worship to a Dragon King shrine: this shallow, five-bay Tang hall offers a different scale and purpose.
itemReasons.foguang: Seven bays, a hipped roof and two rings of columns reveal the scale and spatial layers of a large Tang hall, in contrast to Nanchan's small hall.
itemReasons.tiantai: This hall was long counted among Tang buildings. Later Tang inscriptions prompted its reassessment; the catalog follows a Five Dynasties dating while retaining the debate.

name: Eight Great Liao Timber Structures
eyebrow: Liao timber · North and Northeast China
lede: Few Liao-dynasty timber buildings survive, and enthusiasts call them the “Eight Great Liao Timber Structures”: the Guanyin Pavilion and Main Gate of Dule Temple, the Mahavira Hall of Fengguo Temple, the Mahavira Hall of Kaishan Temple, the Manjushri Hall of Geyuan Temple, the Bhagavat Sutra Repository Hall of Huayan Temple, the Mahavira Hall of Shanhua Temple and the Yingxian Wooden Pagoda.
note: Eight entries correspond to eight surviving timber buildings. The destroyed San Dashi Hall of Guangji Temple is excluded.
selectionReason: A gate, worship halls, a scripture hall, a pavilion and a timber pagoda share this Liao list. Their different uses and scales show how timber frames accommodate passage, worship, scriptures and stacked floors.

itemReasons.geyuan: Its nearly square, three-bay plan and deep eaves introduce Liao construction at a smaller scale; the windows and doors retain components from several periods.
itemReasons.dule_guanyin: Its floors are arranged around a towering Guanyin. Two visible stories conceal an additional structural level, rewarding a closer look at the pavilion's construction.
itemReasons.dule_gate: At Dule Temple, compare this three-bay entrance with the tall image pavilion: the same Liao rebuilding served two very different spatial purposes.
itemReasons.fengguo: A nine-bay hall houses a row of seven Buddhas. Relating its broad roof to the figures inside gives the monumental scale a human reference.
itemReasons.kaishan: Only four interior columns serve this five-bay hall. Look beyond the exterior to see how omitting and shifting columns opens the worship space.
itemReasons.huayan_bojia: Its role as a scripture hall brought architectural wall cabinets and miniature heavenly pavilions into the interior, adding fine joinery to the list's large timber frames.
itemReasons.yingxian: Shift from broad halls to an octagonal timber pagoda, where visible and hidden levels alternate to stack space vertically.
itemReasons.shanhua_daxiong: The seven-bay hall preserves its Liao core alongside Jin repairs and sculpture, showing how later building work and art became part of a Liao monument.

name: Zhuozhang River Valley
lede: The Zhuozhang River runs through the valleys around Pingshun and Lucheng. Villages along its banks preserve a dense cluster of small temples and shrines from the Five Dynasties to the Yuan, making it the classic heritage route of southeast Shanxi.
note: Only valley monuments already in this catalog are listed, in chronological order; a trip can follow the valley from west to east or the reverse.
selectionReason: Follow one valley through Five Dynasties halls, Song and Jin temples, and Yuan shrines. Similar three-bay fronts conceal different roofs, columns and courtyard uses: carry one question from place to place.

itemReasons.longmen: Begin with the Five Dynasties west side hall and its gabled roof, then place it within a temple built across many periods.
itemReasons.tiantai: This small Five Dynasties hall's nearly square plan and simple eave supports make a useful comparison with Longmen and Dayun.
itemReasons.dayun: Five Dynasties murals survive inside a hall of the same period, connecting the timber frame with the painted setting for worship.
itemReasons.yuanqi_hall: This small Song hall stands with Qinglong Pagoda, taking the view from a single timber building to a temple composed of hall and tower.
itemReasons.fotou: A three-bay hall brings together an older timber frame and later murals; read their different dates rather than assigning one period to everything.
itemReasons.yuanqi_qinglong: This octagonal, seven-tier brick pagoda represents timber brackets in brick, adding a change of material to a route dominated by wooden halls.
itemReasons.huilong: Octagonal stone columns mark the front of this three-bay gabled hall. Compare its entrance with Xiayu Shrine in the same village.
itemReasons.chunhua: A single long beam spans front to rear eaves in this three-bay Jin hall, posing a structural question: how can a deeper hall use fewer interior supports?
itemReasons.jiutian: The illustrated Yuan offering hall is open on all sides between a stage and the main hall, introducing a space that links ritual and performance.
itemReasons.xiayu: A deep porch fronts the Yuan main hall, with a Ming gate-stage and Qing side buildings in the same courtyard: a place to connect building dates with uses.
